title: Azure workload scaling strategies
description: Choose the right scaling approach for Azure workloads. Understand vertical scaling, horizontal scaling, autoscale rules, and how to configure scaling for App Service, AKS, and SQL Database.

data.text: Workloads rarely run at a constant load. User traffic spikes at 9 AM, batch jobs run at midnight, and marketing campaigns can double your request rate unexpectedly. Scaling ensures your application remains responsive without over-provisioning resources during quiet periods.

Vertical scaling increases the size of an existing instance—more CPU, more memory, faster disks. Horizontal scaling increases the number of instances. In Azure, vertical scaling usually means resizing an App Service plan or VM, while horizontal scaling means adding instances to a scale set, App Service plan, or AKS cluster.

cards.title: Vertical scaling (scale up)
cards.description: Good for stateful services that cannot run multiple copies, such as a single SQL server. Limited by hardware maximums and requires downtime or restart.

cards.title: Horizontal scaling (scale out)
cards.description: Good for stateless web tiers and microservices. Works with load balancers and container orchestrators. Preferred pattern for cloud-native applications.

data.text: Azure Autoscale automatically adjusts instance counts based on rules or schedules. It supports metric-based rules, such as scaling out when CPU exceeds 70%, and time-based schedules, such as scaling up at 8 AM on weekdays. Autoscale works with App Service, Cloud Services, VMSS, and some other resource types.

data.title: Autoscale profile in ARM JSON
data.content: This profile scales out an App Service plan when CPU is above 70% and scales in when CPU drops below 30%.

data.text: Stateful services such as Azure SQL Database and Cosmos DB scale differently. SQL Database scales by increasing the compute tier or adding read replicas. Cosmos DB scales by increasing throughput (RU/s) or adding partition keys to distribute load. Both support autoscale, but the triggers and limits are specific to the service.

data.title: Scaling rules of thumb
items: Stateless web APIs should scale out horizontally behind a load balancer.
Databases should scale up first, then out via read replicas or partitioning.
Use scheduled scaling for predictable load patterns to avoid cold-start latency.
Set instance limits to prevent runaway costs from misconfigured rules.

data.title: Scaling is not free
data.text: Horizontal scaling introduces complexity around session state, cache coherence, and database connection limits. Make sure your application is stateless before relying on scale-out to fix performance problems.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Horizontal scaling is preferred for stateless cloud workloads.
Azure Autoscale supports both metric-based and schedule-based rules.
Stateful services require service-specific scaling strategies.
Always test scaling rules with realistic traffic patterns.
data.takeaway: Scale the right dimension—out for stateless tiers, up or partition for stateful ones.
